metadata.description:
In today’s episode of our Jharkhand Food Series, we journeyed to an interior village in Netarhat to experience the cuisine of the Asur-Birjia tribe, known as the real forest foragers. We were accompanied by our hosts Dr. Manisha Oraon and Kumar Abhishek Oraon, the co-founders of Open Farm and culinary researcher Jyoti.

There we met Virginia Birjia, who showed us some of the essential greens that form a core part of their daily diet. These foraged treasures included dried mango, dried bamboo shoots, and a variety of exotic greens, each holding unique nutritional benefits and cultural significance. 

From there, we stepped into her kitchen, a modest space where meals are prepared over a traditional wood fire. The first dish she demonstrated was a simple omelette cooked in a leaf bowl, placed directly on the fire. The result was a rustic delicacy infused with smoky flavour.

As we conversed, Virginia explained the tribe’s eating habits, which are deeply rooted in simplicity-minimal oil, almost no spices, native grains, and seasonal produce. The daily meal is mostly vegetarian. Meat, on the other hand, is consumed sparingly, as it is costly for them and reserved mostly for special occasions.

She went on to prepare two remarkable chutneys: one with brahmi saag and the other with dried sanai ke phool. Alongside, there were dishes already prepared: maar jhor, fresh bamboo shoot stir fry, sanai ke phool ki sabzi, arhar dal, and bora saag chutney.

When it was time to eat, the soulful spread was served on leaf plates-a sustainable practice still followed in the community. Over the meal, Abhishek shared valuable insights into the tribe’s way of life, their relationship with the forest, and the nutritional wisdom embedded in their food culture. Every bite carried the essence of the land-simple, nourishing, and deeply fulfilling.
